claims.poster_quote: Reports often explicitly identify invaded organs, but these observations are incomplete because subtle or equivocal extension may be omitted.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: In practice, however, radiologists typically report only obvious and clinically salient invasion, hence subtle or equivocal extension may be omitted.

claims.text: REG uses report evidence to refine, rather than replace, anatomy-based connectivity.
claims.poster_quote: REG therefore uses report evidence to refine, rather than replace, anatomy-based connectivity.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Specifically, we design a Report-Enhanced Graph-Refinement (REG) module that reuses the global report representation as a text node in the graph, employs a large language model (LLM) to identify which organs are explicitly described as invaded in the report, and connects this text node only to primary sites and to those invaded organs, while keeping the original organ–organ edges unchanged.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that REG uses report evidence to refine, rather than replace, anatomy-based connectivity.

claims.text: The proposed framework combines CT-derived organ features with organ-specific evidence from radiology reports.

claims.paper_evidence: We cast laryngopharyngeal cancer T-staging as prediction over an anatomy-structured organ graph that combines CT-derived organ features with organ-level textual cues.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the framework combines CT-derived organ features with organ-specific evidence from radiology reports.

claims.text: The framework contains three components: Anatomy-Structured Organ Graph (AOG), Organ-Anchored Cross-Modal Alignment (OCA), and Report-Enhanced Graph-Refinement (REG).

claims.text: Existing computer-aided approaches underrepresent the anatomy-structured pattern of tumor spread.

claims.paper_evidence: Existing methods underrepresent anatomically structured patterns of tumor invasion, as they either process whole CT volumes without tumor-specific anatomical constraints or rely on labor-intensive tumor segmentation.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that existing computer-aided approaches underrepresent the anatomy-structured pattern of tumor spread.

claims.text: Manual tumor segmentation is costly and difficult because tumors have heterogeneous appearances.

claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that conventional multimodal methods fuse global CT and report representations, making it difficult to align individual anatomical structures with their corresponding textual findings.
